extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism/media studies and journalism practitioners interested in newsroom organization and norms
extracted.subtask_description: Norms and practical standards governing reporters' daily work in a city-hall newspaper bureau: how they locate and claim stories, manage specialties vs. general assignments, share or hoard information, and interact with editors, colleagues, competitors, and sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility / Specialties are ignored when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialties are ignored when necessary. Everyone must be capable of doing everyone else’s work; each specialist must also be a generalist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a reporter may write a colleague’s civil-service column if that colleague is ill; a fiscal specialist may be sent on a late-breaking political story; reporters are routinely asked "Are you up?" and expected to take assignments outside their territory. The ultimate aim: get the work done; rigid adherence to specialty can leave gaps in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalism as getting a story that meets organizational needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Among reporters, professionalism is knowing how to get a story that meets organizational needs and standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence is demonstrated by the ability to file a story every day. Senior reporters are regularly asked by the bureau chief, "What do you have today?" — an expectation that reporters can generate publishable copy from their sources and placement in the news net.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowing sources: locating stories via a bank of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Being a reporter means knowing how to find stories pertinent to one's placement in the news net; locating stories requires having news sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters cultivate a bevy of sources to maximize the ability to file daily. Newcomers must learn 'who's who' both in the newsroom and at City Hall. Sources enable reporters to develop leads, map aspects of running stories over days, and generate exclusives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources confer status (Matthew Effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The higher the status of sources and the greater the scope of their positions, the higher the status of the reporters; 'the more one has, the more one gets.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-status reporters receive 'big stories' more often (even breaching specialties). Example: star reporters get privileged access and frequent good stories, generating envy among less-connected colleagues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources as private property / hoarding information
rubrics_metrics.description: Privately generated ideas or information are treated as the explicit property of their originator; reporters hoard private sources to maintain autonomy and control of their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norms discourage asking colleagues for the names of concealed sources; reporters expect to be given credit for leads they develop and will complain if a source's information is treated as someone else's. This ownership extends to exclusives arranged at social events or via private contacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sharing readily available information with competitors
rubrics_metrics.description: Readily available or easily gleaned information is commonly shared with reporters from other outlets; privately developed information rarely is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: briefing a wire-service reporter about a closed meeting's outcome if a newsroom briefing is expected; exchanging standard factual items like bond interest rates across the press room. Sharing is governed by collegiality and practical expectations about who 'will have' the information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional courtesy and 'contracts' for intra-bureau exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal exchanges or 'contracts' between bureaus and reporters (promises of reciprocal help) are used to obtain information efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a Queens bureau chief requests City Hall reporters to fetch Consumer Affairs data with an understood future reciprocation. These arrangements function like medical consultations—quick, reciprocal, and aiding organizational needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional autonomy can trump organizational diktats
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters exercise autonomy through complex informal codes that may contravene formal organizational directives about sharing and information control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors often cannot directly observe reporters' behavior; they judge competence by published copy and gossip. Reporters may share with competitors and hoard from their own bureau to preserve control and career mobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territoriality and inter-bureau respect
rubrics_metrics.description: Territorial boundaries between bureaus (e.g., City Hall vs. Albany) are recognized; violations are handled with professional courtesy rather than formal hierarchical discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: when the City Hall bureau called state legislators, the Albany chief reprimanded Adams directly by phone to reestablish boundaries rather than escalating to the city editor. Respecting territory protects sources as private property and prevents poaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collegial exchange of minor factual help to speed production
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters routinely ask colleagues small factual questions (spellings, middle initials, standard figures) and expect quick answers to maintain workflow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such exchanges save time, preserve writing rhythm, and serve organizational needs of getting copy in on deadline; they also signal membership and helpfulness within the press-room culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sharing as verification vs. propagation of inaccuracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Reportorial sharing is sometimes justified as verification, but it can also perpetuate inaccuracies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sociological observations note that while sharing may corroborate facts, it can spread errors; denied access to shared info may force reporters to develop new lines of inquiry and possibly better stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural participation increases access to sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation in press-room culture (nicknames, parties, 'Inner Circle' activities) signals insider status and increases familiarity with sources and colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the 'right' nickname or being included in social rituals shows personal acquaintance, which can translate into better information flow and invitations to write certain pieces or enter exclusive networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadlines have cascading organizational consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Missing a reporter's deadline can delay typesetters, cause overtime pay, delay distribution trucks, lose readers to competitors, and reduce circulation and advertising revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'hack saw' logic underpins the organizational imperative for flexibility: reporters must be able to produce copy on time, which justifies sharing, stepping outside specialties, and other adaptive practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of sources privileges powerful, centralized actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters tend to seek centralized sources—politicians, bureaucrats, leaders of political clubs—not grassroots activists; they prioritize sources with actual power and resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This orientation influences what information is uncovered and reported, privileging perspectives of those with institutional power (see cross-reference to chapter 5 for consequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowing what questions to ask / figuring the 'heart' of the matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must know what questions to ask a source and what facts to find; having some idea of the story's 'heart' is necessary to elicit useful information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without a sense of the central issue, interviews and fact-gathering are unfocused and less likely to yield publishable material; experienced reporters use their sense of the 'heart' to guide source questioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity and reputation affect mobility and cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: A reputation for professional sharing and helpfulness enhances occupational mobility and the warmth with which one is greeted by new colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters who cooperate at scenes, share information when appropriate, and participate in press-room culture are more likely to be assisted in future and to carry those reputational benefits when moving between organizations.
